We've developed a technique to automate the dilation optimization process by casting it as a weight-pruning operation along the time axis. Our method learns dilation factors concurrently with weights during training and achieves notable gains in model compactness and inference efficiency without compromising accuracy. It produces a range of highly optimal TCN variants from a single starting model, surpassing the performance of custom-designed networks in both efficiency and accuracy.

Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct concepts: projection grouping and correspondence learning. A projection grouping module is employed to cluster projected landmarks from multiple views. These modules are integrated by a loss function that enforces correspondence between projected landmarks and control points. Experimental results on the PRS dataset demonstrate superior performance of our proposed approach over several state-of-the-art methods.

This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. We studied an array of Type IIB four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective field theories to uncover the range of universal symmetries potentially present and then investigated why they are avoided. Generalized $\theta$-terms emerge as crucial elements in these theories due to nontrivial applications of the uniqueness theorem. We established that all global symmetries are subject to $\theta$-term-induced elimination. Futhermore, we determined the possible charge assignments for bulk matter fields respecting the global symmetries, which led to the conclusion that the symmetries can be either absent or finite in number on the worldvolume of any possible global symmetry-carrying object with local charge. We offer a deeper application of the $\theta$-term argument as well, demonstrating that the $SU(2)$ R-symmetry must be limited due to the existence of a positive-energy effect that arises from $\theta$-terms in a specific regime.

multi-phonon physics, is driving research and development for both fundamental understanding and applications in metrology and communication systems. Quantum acoustic resonators serve as the ideal testing ground for multi-phonon phenomena through a combination of theoretical and experimental studies. The specific system studied consists of a semiconductor quantum dot driven by a laser, coupled to an acoustic cavity, and has exhibited remarkable multi-phonon properties, albeit previously described with a simplistic two-level quantum dot model. However, by accounting for both bright and dark excitons within the quantum dot model, the complexity of this system can be better represented. The inclusion of dark excitons offers a particular advantage, given their inherently low decoherence rates as a result of lacking spontaneous photon emission. Consequently, researchers are now capable of achieving giant Rabi oscillations between a vacuum state and a dark exciton state accompanied by N-phonon bundles by adjusting the laser frequency with precision. Notably, this breakthrough facilitates the creation of dark states within the quantum dot without relying on an external magnetic field, paving the way for significant advances in this field.

This model contains horizontal and vertical hopping terms that are equal in the vertical direction but relate irreducibly under the non-symmorphic symmetry when the horizontal hopping terms match. As a result, the irreducible representations of this lattice include conical points at the M and X high-symmetry points in the Brillouin zone boundary. We found that most non-symmorphic herringbone lattices will have isolated conical points at the boundary of the 1D Brillouin zone, but certain types will have conical lines appearing along the boundary. We also provide information on the possible material applications of herringbone lattices.

CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To improve the performance of automatic tumor detection, researchers have developed an approach that involves using segmentation models with attention mechanisms and patient-specific data augmentation. In this study, various models with attention layers and training strategies have been compared in terms of their effectiveness. The most effective results were obtained when using the U-Net attention architecture with a attention mechanism placement at the bottleneck, along with an unsupervised pre-training approach based on image reconstruction and feature extraction. This also yielded notable improvements when feeding the reconstructed images and feature maps as well-known disease characteristics such as air pockets and high-density areas through extra channels. Ultimately, this architecture achieved state-of-the-table performance with 97.55% dice score and 98.74% IoU.

addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multi-target cross-domain recommendation in multiple sparse domains. In contrast to conventional CDR methods, MSDCR considers all participating domains as equally data-poor, thereby simultaneously enhancing the recommendation performance across each domain. We devise a Multi-Domain Separation Network (MDSN) and a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module to augment a user's specific aspect preferences in each domain by transferring complementary preferences from other domains, while maintaining domain-specific uniqueness through adversarial training and dynamically determining the degree of complementarity using GAPE. Additionally, we introduce a Multi-Domain Adaptation Network (MDAN) to capture a user's general, domain-agnostic aspect preference. By integrating the domain-specific aspect preference and the domain-agnostic aspect preference, MSDCR attains a thorough understanding of user preferences across each data-poor domain. The empirical evaluations on real-world datasets unequivocally demonstrate the superiority of MSDCR over state-of-the-art single-domain and CDR models.

Pyramid Networks (FPNs), frequently struggle with identifying large-scale objects due to an inherent drawback in the framework. This paper reexamines FPN within the context of detection systems and sheds light on its success through an optimization lens. It identifies that incorporating FPN results in distorted backpropagation pathways, limiting each backbone network level to focus on specific scale ranges. Consequently, two practical approaches are presented to empower each backbone level to consider all objects within the detection framework. Firstly, introducing auxiliary objectives facilitates direct propagation signals during training. Secondly, constructing the feature pyramid more reasonably can circumvent irrational backpropagation paths. Comprehensive experiments validate the analysis and demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed methods on the COCO benchmark, resulting in substantial improvements of over 2% across one-stage, two-stage, anchor-based, anchor-free, and transformer-based detectors.

Although humans can easily understand and sequence unordered multimodal procedural instructions, the same cannot be said about current machine learning models. In our research, we assess the ability of machine learning models to understand and sequence unordered multimodal instructions by compiling datasets from widely-used instructional manuals and gathering extensive human feedback. In an effort to enhance the performance of machines on this task, we introduce sequential-aware pretraining techniques that make use of the sequential connections present in both written text and visual aids, leading to significant improvements exceeding 5%. As a supplementary benefit, these methods also enhance other related tasks such as multimodal instruction following.

Researchers often study network immunization, but traditional approaches typically focus on broad measures, such as network criticality and component size. In contrast, this paper delves into a micro-level analysis, where the removal of individual nodes during an attack is examined in detail. Based on percolation theory, the authors analyze the effects of removing a single node that causes other nodes to disconnect from the main component. A widely accepted evaluation standard in software testing is mutation analysis, assessing the ability to detect artificial faults, yet this method is not commonly applied to fuzzing. We propose incorporating mutation analysis as a means to evaluate the performance of fuzzers, addressing the lack of a standard benchmark. We present guidelines to adapt mutation analysis for evaluating fuzzers, addressing specific differences. A key challenge we addressed is the correlation between the ability to benchmark mutations and the detection of actual faults. We found a significant impact, with the presence of real bugs able to reveal many otherwise undetectable mutations. A potential solution involved separating performance across multiple categories: the detection of real bugs, detection of mutations that can be reached, and detection of mutations that, when present, would be exposed by the fuzzer. We examined several leading fuzzers, including AFL++, SEED, and Z3Coverage, using 14 programs and found that they had similar abilities to detect bugs, but varied in their ability to detect reachable mutations. As a result, we suggest assessing fuzzer performance primarily through their ability to detect mutations that could be considered a standard benchmark.

we studied a distant starburst galaxy, examining how star formation-driven gas outflows are linked to other properties of the galaxy. Researchers have a rich history of developing and analyzing preservation-based discretization techniques for well-established equations such as Poise-Boussinesq and Cahn-Navier-Stokes systems. However, preserving the maximum principle in time-dependent elliptic Helmholtz problems has received little attention, especially regarding the development of discrete maximum principle (DMP)-compliant methods. Our work addresses this gap by presenting time-stepping schemes that ensure DMP for solutions of the elliptic Helmholtz problem. Specifically, we focus on theories and experiments for solutions to a boundary value problem where we need to find u such that $-\Delta u + uu = f$ with given boundary conditions $\gamma u = \varphi$. To achieve this, we decompose the problem into four sub-domains and limit the time-step size $\Delta t$ based on the norm of the source term f. Our numerical results support theoretical findings, demonstrating the first instance of a finite difference method complying with DMP for solving the elliptic Helmholtz problem.

Moreover, we introduce a multi-branch detection head that leverages the specificity of different modalities to produce accurate bounding box predictions. These features give R-VNet the ability to accurately detect objects at far-field distances. Experimental evaluations on the nuScenes dataset demonstrate that our method yields significant improvements in detection accuracy compared to both baseline methods and state-of-the-art techniques. As a result, R-VNet can effectively detect objects at far-field distances.

We've established conditions under which the method converges to the true reachable set boundary by ensuring the discretization grid is sufficiently fine, especially around regions where the optimal value function exhibits steep gradients. shed new light on the ultimate demise of massive stars, contradicting widely accepted theoretical models. The author proposes a novel scenario for the internal shock waves generated near the onset of core contraction. When a star's rotation is slow and the magnetic field isn't dominant, a universal pattern of internal shock waves emerges. These shock waves are comprised of distinct 'islands' that persist regardless of the original structure of the proto-neutron star. The most prominent island generates a strong, persistent spiral shock, capable of expelling the entire star if it hasn't already collapsed due to rotation or dominance of magnetic fields. Observations of supernovae and hypernovovae can be explained by this scenario, with the observed axisymmetry a direct result of the extracted angular momentum. However, this internal shock mechanism may be incapable of causing the ultra-relativistic outflows observed in some superbright supernovae and hypernovovovae.

unclonable encryption, a unique feature in an encryption scheme where an adversary can't produce two encrypted versions of the same original message from a given ciphertext. Our research expands upon this concept, focusing on several aspects:

  - Flexibility in Usage: We've identified a significant drawback in the previous unclonable encryption constructions by Broadbent and Lord, as they either only guarantee single-use security in the plain model or security in the random oracle model. Our research presents two novel constructions for both public-key and private-key settings that maintain security even after repeated use and are founded on minimal assumptions.

  - Understanding Cloning Capacity: We've investigated the one-time secure construction proposed by Broadbent and Lord, specifically aiming to determine if achieving a nearly optimal $0.5^n$ success probability for cloning is attainable. Our findings generalize the construction based on various forms of monogamy of entanglement and present attacks against specific schemes with cloning probabilities reaching as high as $0.75^n$.

  - Applications to Copy Protection: We've discovered that strong forms of unclonable encryption can lead to enhanced security, specifically copy-protection for unlearnable functions. Our research paves the way for potential new constructions meeting these requirements, thereby expanding the realm of copy-protection methods.

often regulated or redirected by magnetic fields that create a surrounding

This paper explores the link between CT and advanced computer systems that identify relationships within a text. By developing specific metrics and a search-based method, the study examines if modern computer systems that recognize connections within a text align with the principles of CT. The analysis indicates a correlation between the systems' ability to recognize connections and their ability to model the coherence of the text, but also reveals that these computer systems are not necessarily improved by considering the ideas underlying CT. By incorporating these elements, the study presents a revised version of CT and shows that it enhances the performance of the computer systems in recognizing connections within the text.

, cutting-edge experiments employing long-baseline neutrino detection systems rely heavily on the development of detailed models describing the interactions between neutrinos and atomic nuclei. The intricacy of these models is significant, partly because existing detectors have been incapable of observing final state neutrons, which has led to significant systematic uncertainties. The implementation of 3D scintillator tracking technology in next-generation long-baseline neutrino experiments has improved detection capabilities by enabling event-by-event measurement of neutron kinetic energy resulting from neutrino interactions, thus providing valuable information for refining neutrino interaction models and reconstructing neutrino energies. Prototypes of these detectors have undergone neutron irradiation at the LANL beamline in both 2019 and 2020. The primary goal was to demonstrate the ability to detect neutrons within the neutrino interaction range. The results from this study provide a detailed description of the relationship between the measured kinetic energy and that of Monte Carlo simulations, which can contribute to a deeper understanding of quantum chromodynamic functions used in related frameworks. Findings have revealed that the proposed method of analyzing data can reduce measurement uncertainties for neutrino interaction cross sections, and have also yielded the first direct evidence of charge asymmetry when comparing neutron and charged current deep inelastic scattering.

Employing a quantum Monte Carlo dynamical cluster approximation, we analyzed the effects of Rashba spin-orbit coupling and Zeeman field on superconductivity in a two-dimensional attractive Hubbard model with doping. Our findings reveal that Rashba coupling enhances s-wave superconductivity's $T_c$ maximum, which occurs near neutral points in momentum space. Notably, Rashba coupling facilitates the coexistence of superconductivity and Zeeman-field-induced charge density wave within the same strong superconducting region. graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of high-quality crystalline materials by embedding graphene within other compound structures. However, most related studies have been limited to anecdotal evidence due to constraints in graphene's growth location. Overcoming these limitations is possible with a new proposed experimental setup designed to grow graphene directly on top-sealed silicon wafer lids, which can then be incorporated into doped bulk silicon substrates through cutting and grinding. This method of 'internal remote epitaxy' offers unique advantages, including better control of doping levels in the embedded graphene and enhanced thermal stability due to isolated growth conditions. As a result, embedded graphene within silicon exhibits moderated doping levels, allowing for electric field modulation of its properties later on. The inclusion of phosphorus atoms within the graphene layer was confirmed with high precision using atomistic imaging and chemical analysis techniques. Based on detailed analyses, a carrier mobility of approximately 10,000 $cm^2/Vs$ at room temperature was achieved on these internally remotely epitaxial doped graphene samples, demonstrating their high electrical performance.

high energy radiation remains a mystery.  Hadronic radiation emission can offer a potential explanation.  By analyzing the relationship between gamma-rays and radio waves, researchers discovered evidence of hadronic-pion decay resulting in radio waves.  The intensity of radiation would be produced at the boundary where protons interact with electrons to create positrons.  The intensity of radiation was calculated and the electron energy was adjusted to obtain gamma-ray spectra similar to observed spectra.  It was discovered that under observational constraints, approximately 30 to 300 percent of energy from protons could be converted into radiation.  However, this mechanism appears insufficient to fully account for observed emissions.  Nevertheless, electron energy loss calculations revealed that hadronic processes could explain observed emissions in Tycho's Nova from a thousand years ago, as well as the massive star remnant Cassiopeia.

Although various calibration techniques have been developed to tackle this problem, they often struggle to maintain good generalization performance on unseen data. While several generalization theory research papers have made significant contributions, they've mainly focused on well-calibrated models and haven't thoroughly investigated the generalized error's dependencies on models' generalized accuracy and expected confidence. Our Generalized Error Formula successfully links a model's generalized error to its generalized accuracy, generalized $k$-times mean confidence, and other factors for any $l_2$-norm-based margin. Generalizing the results from prior work, the formula comprehensively encompasses the error bounds from several famous models like SVM, Softmax, and more. This research framework can be utilized to establish new generalization upper bounds for various models and provide a unified perspective on the effects of different factors on generalized $k$-times mean confidence. This formula's utility is validated through experimental verification on multiple image datasets.

While previous SPADE approaches have been theoretical or based on approximations of the point spread function (PSF), practical implementations require precise knowledge of the positions of overlapping sources. In a novel approach, we utilize the Fourier transform of the PSF (RTPADE) in the real domain to collect field information maximally. The RTPADE approach overcomes the need for precise source positioning and outperforms the Rayleigh criterion in practical scenarios by a significant margin (1.37 times the traditional limit). The results of the RTPADE approach may have broad implications, including the development of more efficient optical systems for source localization and the foundation for the practical application of quantum radar systems that distinguish weak signals from background noise.

This paper focuses on a model consisting of a two-level ecosystem where two species of predators, competing for a common prey, engage in explicit interference. The model is reworked to display a singular perturbation with rapid prey movement and slower predator movement, allowing for a regime close to the singular Hopf bifurcation to be analyzed. Near this point, the model exhibits chaotic, mixed-mode oscillations, consisting of long-lasting, concatenated periods of small and large amplitude movements. These eventually transition into the model's steady-state equilibrium. To determine the initiating factors behind a large amplitude oscillation in the mixed-mode orbit, the model is reduced to a suitable normal form, located at the singular Hopf point. The resulting normal form reveals a separating surface that distinguishes two forms of oscillations, and the occurrence of a large amplitude oscillation depends on whether the trajectory crosses from the 'inner' to the 'outer' side of this boundary. Conditions derived from the normal form can predict whether the model will enter another period of MMO behavior before reaching equilibrium. These conditions may serve as early warning indicators for a population shift in the ecosystem. The conditions are also examined within the context of the full model and demonstrated numerally.

A previously developed approach by Baker achieved PTAS on various graph classes including planar graphs. Further, Romero, Wrochna, and Zivny developed a simpler PTAS for certain graph classes using the Sherali-Adams LP relaxation for maximum CSPs with constraints defined by arbitrary non-negative functions.

This research is extended to CSPs with constraints that have multiple possible values. The only restriction for such constraints is that they contain an element that is at least as acceptable as all other elements.

A new PTAS is presented for general-valued CSPs with constraints that have distinct values, such as 0 and 1, but with specific limitations. The technique was previously applicable to classes where Baker's approach worked, except possibly fractionally-treewidth-fragile classes. The findings relax the monotonicity condition for constraints, allowing a new property called "list-colorability".

rotation pattern within a less massive and less luminous star that has evolved into a giant. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect a faster core rotation rate compared to their outer layers. Contrary to these expectations, KIC 9267654's rotation speed is observed to be higher near its surface rather than at its core. To address this discrepancy, we developed a non-LTE atmospheric model of this star's spectrum at 600-700 nm, identifying key spectral characteristics indicative of its rotation, including broad H-alpha lines and distinct absorption features linked to its internal rotation. Our results place the core and surface of KIC 9267654 as unusually rapid rotators for a star of its type and mass, presenting a potential challenge to current atmospheric modeling and stellar evolution models.

Although machine learning models have been successful in detecting false information, especially when large amounts of labeled data are available, their effectiveness significantly declines when they are applied to emerging events. This limitation creates a significant obstacle for the current methods in detecting false news on unexpected events. Furthermore, the fact that newly emerging events necessitate building a new model from scratch or retraining the existing one from beginning to end, which is both a costly and time-consuming process. To address this challenge, in this paper, we propose an end-to-end neural network architecture called MetaLearn, that utilizes meta-learning to automatically identify false information related to unexpected events on Twitter. MetaLearn comprises two key components, namely a teacher network and a student network. The teacher network acquires valuable insights from the initial training samples that include both false and genuine accounts, while the student network learns to distinguish between false and authentic accounts with little to no human assistance. Our experiments demonstrate that MetaLearn outperforms the state-of-the-art baselines, especially in the context of unexpected events, by leveraging high-quality information from social media to create a robust detector of false news through an efficient, automated process.

When particles are confined within a periodic potential, they can migrate from one unit cell to a neighboring cell, requiring the application of an electric field. In this context, we examine Su-Schrieffer-Heeger models, where electrons are paired with phonons, to explore how tunneling can be observed. By analyzing total occupation over specific sites, we seek to identify the conditions and signatures of quantum tunneling in this system. When the external electric field is either suddenly applied or gradually changed, we find that in a periodic arrangement without external influences, a distinct pattern of charge transfer, known as charge pumping, occurs, representing the system's quantum tunneling behavior. Moreover, we propose that quantum tunneling and charge pumping can be observed and measured in carbon nanotubes arranged in rings, coupled with atomic sites, by monitoring the time-dependent charge within a specific site when a voltage is applied at a specific point.

Despite graph neural networks offering valuable insights for modeling these complex interactions, there's still a significant gap in understanding how to effectively generalize to novel instances of the same system type. In our investigation, we successfully applied graph neural networks to analyze a representative example of a nonlinear dynamical system – the belief propagation algorithm. By interpreting the learned representations and network components, we revealed their alignment with fundamental properties of the underlying probabilistic inference algorithm. Laser Interstitial Thermal Therapy (LITT) treats seizures caused by epilepsy in a specific brain area, the mesial temporal lobe. Evaluating the effectiveness of this treatment requires analyzing changes to the treated brain area after LITT, which can be achieved by accurately defining the treated region through image processing. Although deep learning techniques offer high precision in defining this region, training them requires a large amount of data which can be hard to obtain for a new and emerging treatment such as LITT. Therefore, a change learning framework called Reversible Network Distillation (ReNetD) was developed to efficiently utilize existing knowledge from other thermal therapy treatments and apply it to the new treatment, in this case, by transferring information from Free Space Network (FSN) to a cutting-edge model called Unsupervised Boundary Network (UnBNet). By pretraining the FSN and gradually modifying its neural structure to fit the requirements of the task at hand, high precision and performance can be achieved with limited data, in this case, by extracting features from 30 epilepsy cases from the mesial temporal lobe after LITT treatment, a combination of Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) and Magnetic Resonance Encephalography (MREEG) images were processed using the proposed change learning framework, resulting in an average Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) of 0.782 and an average Hausdorff Distance (HD95) of 8.781 mm. This paper assesses the effectiveness and efficiency of a method to coordinate astrobots in the SDSS-V by running numerous simulated and real-world tests. We demonstrate that our approach establishes a complete coordination framework based on the specific features and configurations of astrobots, their objectives, and operating parameters. To optimize the algorithm, a method involving cooperative artificial forces is used to create safe, coherent trajectories for the astrobots, leading to faster convergence and reduced oscillatory movements. Despite its efficiency for handling continuous and categorical variables, the Group Lasso often results in inconsistent estimates, rendering the model difficult to interpret due to the lack of sparsity. To achieve a sparse solution using the Group Lasso while capturing the data's categorical structure, we propose an innovative approach that splits each high-cardinality category into its constituent levels and applies the Sparse Auto-Encoder (SAE) to the Group Lasso's penalty matrix's low-rank decomposition. By leveraging the dimensionality reduction power of the SAE for continuous variables and using the SAE's derivative to derive a smooth and continuous low-dimensional representation of the categorical variables' levels, our method seamlessly integrates categorical and continuous variables' representations. Our approach's unique ability to handle the Group Lasso's low-rank assumptions and yield a sparse solution makes it a versatile tool for dimension reduction, feature selection, and model regularization. Our experimental results on real-world datasets underscore the SAE-GP Lasso's performance in dimension reduction, feature selection, and model regularization.

Current methods of weather prediction, using either a network of sensors or a vehicle-mounted camera, are limited in scope and costly.
A robust weather detection system is crucial for seamless operation of transportation services in diverse weather conditions.

A key finding reveals that networks comprising a single type of tensor and possessing good code properties can only model systems with a local Hamiltonian if the network's depth is limited to two layers. Additionally, it has been proven that for networks with three or more layers, the entanglement entropy exhibits only a quadratic dependence on the network's boundary size, thereby precluding the possibility of area-law behavior in Hamiltonians that can be described by such networks. However, our results also show that networks with a three-layer structure provide the minimal complexity required for the emergence of power-law scaling. A novel, general class of symmetric tensors is introduced that results in logarithmic entropy for such networks, which can be slightly expanded upon to yield power-law entropy with a specific, controllable exponent. This format can also be used to design networks that support topological order. Such networks can, in turn, be mapped to a Kogut-Susskind lattice through a process known as 1-gauge theory transformation.

Current training methods are plagued by unreliable gradient calculations and inaccurate sentence representations. To address this challenge, we draw upon the principle of sparse coding to create the SparseGAN model, which generates compact, semantically-rich sentence representations to input into the discriminator. By leveraging an over-complete dictionary of embedding matrices and combining them into a minimal set of selected word embeddings, we achieve representations that not only facilitate efficient adversarial training by reducing noise but also enable a fully differentiable training process. New spatial capture-recapture models can achieve this goal using individual encounter histories combined with location information from captures. We present a statistical method that integrates capture data from various sources with telemetry data to model these components jointly and provides a likelihood-based estimation model for SCR parameters using capture data and environmental covariates. compatibility conditions, an operator with which it is invariant when applied to a given differential equation, is known as the direct problem. This process yields successive first-order operators for an n-dimensional manifold. The converse, an inverse problem, is to find the original differential operator when one of these compatibility operators is known. The compatibility operator can be parameterized by the original differential operator only if it defines a torsion-free differential module. The parametrization is minimal when this differential module has a vanishing differential rank. Notably, attempts to parameterize the Cauchy stress operator have been a subject of study for renowned scientists such as G.B. Airy, J.C. Maxwell, and A. Einstein. This work identifies a widespread misconception among them, mistakenly using the Einstein operator and confusing it with the Cauchy operator and the $div$ operator induced from the Bianchi operator. As an interesting aside, determining whether Einstein was aware of previous work is a historical puzzle.

We specifically studied three key aspects during this period: the daily management and leadership style of Oort; the sources of funding for the laboratory; and the development of research programs. During Oort's time as director, the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory experienced considerable growth, which ultimately culminated in major expansions during the 1960s. We discovered that although the 1960s led to significant physical and personnel growth at the laboratory, the research programs and funding sources for the laboratory were thoughtfully established during the period we examined. Oort's approach to laboratory management was unique, given his willingness to engage with the mundane aspects of daily management, often surpassing the level of involvement typically seen in leadership roles. His primary motivations for this level of engagement were his desire to maximize the efficiency of the laboratory, his enjoyment of the subject matter, and his enjoyment of interacting with the laboratory's staff. Oort's collaborative and trusting leadership style, characterized by his willingness to engage with the work being done within the laboratory, fostered a highly productive and fulfilling working environment for the laboratory's scientists.

Focusing on the varying effects of remote learning on diverse demographic groups, data was collected from online learning modules in the Fall 2020 and Spring 2020 semesters. Three indicators measured students' ability to stay on track: module start time, on-time module completion, and on-time assignment submission. Findings from a logistic regression model, controlling for other factors, revealed that university students who learned remotely in the Fall 2020 semester had a 10% higher likelihood of starting modules on time and a 12% higher likelihood of submitting assignments on time, but also exhibited lower module completion rates (8% lower likelihood). Contrary to initial expectations, university students who learned remotely due to the COVID pandemic in the Spring 2020 semester showed no significant difference in these behaviors when compared to those who learned remotely before the pandemic. Furthermore, university students who learned remotely in the Fall 2020 semester were found to be younger, more likely to be female, and had lower family income levels. University students who struggled to keep up with the pace of instruction were found to be older, more likely to be male, and had higher family income levels. These results suggest that some segments of the university student population may be disproportionately affected by the difficulties of remote learning.

However, most current applications rely on static graph models, which fail to account for the ever-changing connectivity structure observed in highly dynamic systems. Utilizing static models in such scenarios leads to suboptimal performance. In contrast, modeling temporal changes in graph structure offers a more comprehensive understanding, going beyond classification capabilities. Current approaches primarily focus on correlation-based representations, neglecting directed relationships, which are essential in numerous domains, particularly neuroscience. Our novel model, DECENNT, seeks to address this limitation by introducing a directed and dynamic graph, where nodes represent brain regions and edges capture their mutual interactions. Training DECENNT on fMRI data, we achieved state-of-the-art performance on multiple datasets for regression tasks, including connectivity reconstruction and neural signal generation. Our experiments demonstrate DECENNT's potential to handle temporal changes in graph structure effectively, an essential feature for a more accurate and functional understanding of neural processes.

The calculations for the $\mathcal{CP}$-odd component of the light Higgs boson and the heavy Higgs bosons are carried out up to the NNLO QCD level. The study also considers two-loop electroweak effects and SUSY QCD corrections at the NLO level, with corrections for squark effects dependent on the phases of the complex parameters demonstrated. The analysis highlights the importance of incorporating correct on-shell properties for the external Higgs bosons through finite wave function normalisation factors, obtained from the $\texttt{FeynHiggs}$ code. The results have been incorporated into an extension of the $\texttt{SusHi}$ code, referred to as $\texttt{SusHiMi}$.

By providing an alternative expression for computing derivatives, this differentiability enables significant reductions in memory requirements, obviating the need for unrolling optimization procedures during backward passes. However, this typically requires the computationally expensive inversion of large Hessian matrices. Two experiments demonstrate the feasibility and memory-saving advantages of this approach.

Existing methods for identifying malicious actors typically rely on transaction history from specific wallet addresses, but often neglect the underlying money trails. As working practices shift to the remote working environment, the risk of sensitive data falling into the wrong hands increases, highlighting the pressing need for more robust and user-friendly encryption methods for unauthorised access prevention. This paper aims to introduce a novel encryption algorithm called NoPass, which enables users to recover their data through the use of a pre-shared secret without needing a password, incorporating a combination of nested file manipulation techniques and cryptographic functions including base64 encoding, file decryption using a one-time password (OTP), and advanced data manipulation methods such as XOR, base64 encoding/decoding, and file swapping. Through extensive experimental analysis, the paper also presents key performance metrics of the proposed NoPass algorithm, focusing on key aspects including data integrity verification, data recovery time, performance metrics in relation to file size, and the impact of file names on performance.

Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. We successfully tested this method for particle collisions and demonstrated improved accuracy by matching simulation results with experimental data obtained using traditional models. Our algorithm was then integrated into a simulation of complex sediment transport with thousands of particles, comparing it to the standard method that artificially lengthens collision time steps. Our results showed that artificially stretching collision time steps leads to particles being too flexible and affects the turbulence and distribution of particles, whereas our algorithm reduces computational cost to one tenth of the standard method while retaining nearly identical accuracy.

is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height. Initially, a simplified model of the robot is developed by treating the ground as part of the system's states. This approach allows for incorporating ground deformation into the system's dynamics. A new control method is then implemented to bring the robot to its desired state without relying on friction between the ground and the robot. The chosen control strategy maps the system's state directly to the input force applied to the leg. This method of control transforms the robot into a spring-mass damper system. The resulting model is simulated in a one-dimensional environment to evaluate the method's effectiveness, which is then applied to a two-dimensional robot with results matching theoretical expectations. The anticipated future work involves incorporating ground deformation into more complex robots.

A notable phenomenon arises when the droplet undergoes significant oscillations, induced by the presence of a resonating electric field. The air circulation patterns that emerge as a result create localized aerodynamic forces that impede the droplet's ability to generate a rupture-induced explosion. considering negation, a fundamental aspect of all human languages. Despite being present in every language, negation poses significant challenges to current natural language processing systems. To accelerate the advancement of models capable of accurately processing negation, we introduce CONDAQA, a pioneering English reading comprehension dataset. It demands that models infer the implications of negated statements within passages, collected from a diverse set of paragraphs featuring varied negation cues. Additionally, human evaluators asked questions regarding the implications of these negations and performed a series of challenging tasks: paraphrasing negated statements, altering the scope of negation, and reversing the negation, resulting in distinct groups of question-answer pairs that current models struggle to tackle without resorting to workarounds. Our CONDAQA dataset comprises 14,182 challenging question-answer pairs, encompassing over 50 unique negation cues and proves particularly demanding for leading NLP models. Notably, these models performed substantially worse on CONDAQA compared to other prominent NLP benchmarks, including the SQuAD 2.0 dataset. By providing access to our dataset and associated evaluation code, we encourage the NLP community to utilize it for assessing model performance.

, with numerous countries enforcing strict lockdowns and millions of lives affected. In an effort to cope with the emotional impact, people are increasingly expressing their sentiments on social media. However, manually analyzing such vast amounts of data is impractical, necessitating the use of advanced sentiment analysis techniques. This research focuses on identifying negative sentiments related to COVID-19 from Facebook comments, employing a pre-trained BERT model fine-tuned for sentiment classification. By leveraging Facebook's API to collect comment data and utilizing the NLTK package for API integration, we obtained a comprehensive dataset of 100,000 comments, which were used to evaluate the performance of our model. The experimental results demonstrated that a fully trained model achieved a training accuracy of 98.88%, whereas a model trained only on negative examples also reached 98.88% accuracy, indicating that a lighter model may be sufficient for such tasks.

interlayer tunneling models were the prominent theoretical concepts to describe cuprate superconductors by connecting CuO planes through Josephson coupling. Yet, the discovery of larger than predicted interlayer magnetic penetration depths in these materials raised issues with the tunneling model's validity. The emergence of planar stripes and charge domains enabled alternative Josephson coupling theories. Our study finds the average intralayer interaction to be greater than interlayer coupling and comparable to condensation energy, ultimately yielding long-range phase order-driven superconductivity. As an outcome, our model predicts enhanced superconductivity at optimal doping and suppression of interlayer tunneling signals. Furthermore, our model offers explanations for observed phenomena including the Nernst effect, magnetic penetration depth, and viscosity of normal fluid in optimal doping cuprate superconductors.

two-dimensional solitons, like those for Bose-Einstein condensates described by the Gross-Pitaevskii equations, have the property of Galilean invariance. This allows for solitons to be moved from a stationary state by incorporating invariance. Researchers face a challenge in finding models capable of exhibiting stable, self-accelerating motion of solitons. Self-accelerating modes are well-documented in linear systems in the form of Airy waves, but these waves exhibit poor localization. This concise analysis presents a pair of two-component Bose-Einstein condensate models which can accurately predict the existence of self-accelerating solitons. One such model, featuring interacting 1D solitons, involves a binary BEC trapped within an optical-lattice potential and utilizes interaction forces with opposite signs to create a balance between nonlinearity and dispersion. The other model, derived from a spatially inhomogeneous system with inhomogeneous interaction and mass parameters, exhibits a specific condition where parameters vary linearly with respect to the condensate's axis, enabling the maintenance of constant acceleration. Both models yield specific self-accelerating soliton solutions that remain stable within a certain range of parameters. This range can be precisely mapped using linear stability analysis and numerical simulations.

a model from distributed data on a graph is a challenging task, especially when it comes to Federated Learning. A significant obstacle in this process is the substantial communication required between nodes and the server. A common strategy used to address this issue involves each node making several local model updates before sharing the updated model with the server. Although this method reduces communication costs, it introduces statistical disparities among the nodes' data sets that can hinder convergence and result in the learning of a model that doesn't accurately represent the entire data set. An alternative is known as zeroth-order local update learning (ZOLU), a new approach in which the server queries the objective function at two points, resulting in full model updates from each node that are aggregated using standard methods. While ZOLU achieves a more homogeneous global model and high quality in the final model, it requires full model re-transmission from each node at each iteration, which defeats the purpose of conducting local updates in terms of communication efficiency. This paper introduces an innovative variant of ZOLU called sparse ZOLU (sZOLU), achieving first-order complexity in terms of communication for the same statistical error bound as ODE. Additionally, when the objective function is strongly convex, sZOLU also reduces variance over time, offering a significant improvement in the algorithm. high-energy Electromagnetic Counterpart All-sky Monitor (GECAM) is to observe various Gamma-Ray Bursts (GRB) that arise from the merger of compact binary stars or the collapse of massive stars, which can also generate gravitational waves. To ensure the performance of GECAM's Gamma-Ray Detectors (GRDs) and test its onboard triggering and localization software before launch, a portable device that simulates Gamma-Ray Bursts (GRBs) has been developed using a grid klystron generator. This klystron-driven $\gamma$-ray simulator produces short-duration bursts of $\gamma$-rays with energies ranging from tens of keV to several MeV, which were detected and recorded by GECAM's GRDs before the satellite's launch. The results show that each GRB simulator's performance was successfully captured by the full-energy detectors and wide-field detectors on GECAM, with parameters including total energy ($E_{\rm tot}$), peak energy ($E_{\rm peak}$), and spectral peak flux ($F_{\rm peak}$) determined and compared. Although the parameters obtained from the GRB simulator do not match natural GRB parameters, they can still provide valuable information to astrophysical researchers.

amplified over the past century through the vast growth of scientific literature. However, despite employing metrics such as citation counts and impact factors, it remains unclear how a discipline's knowledge amount correlates with productivity, specifically how the value of new knowledge varies with each new advancement. To address this question, researchers compiled 185 million articles spanning 19 disciplines and analyzed the citation networks between authors, essentially mapping the evolution of scientific knowledge within each area. Using both structured and unstructured entropies to analyze the resulting data, they devised the Quantitative Index of Knowledge (KQI), which measures knowledge amount as a disorder difference created by increasing order within the scientific literature. Subsequently, they discovered that the growth of new literature accelerates the growth of new knowledge, but there is an evident slowdown before this threshold.

The primary goal of this investigation is to determine optimal power allocation methods across various frequencies in order to enhance end-to-end data transmission security while adhering to power consumption constraints at both the sender and relay nodes. However, our current understanding of LSTMs' internal workings is limited, hindering our ability to optimize their design and develop a more refined theoretical framework for the field. LSTMs' enhanced representational power is largely attributed to their modular design that mimics biological neural systems' functional specialization and modular organization. However, standard LSTM implementations fail to capture this specialized design and rely instead on repeating identical modules. By replacing the standard LSTM structure with a hierarchically organized, specialized neural network, researchers found the Hybrid LSTM (Hi LSTM) model demonstrates a more refined learning process and exhibits enhanced robustness, efficiency, and generalization compared to the original LSTM model. By further combining hi-LSTMs with a Graph Neural Network, HiLSTMs achieve greater accuracy and robustness in graph prediction tasks.

NLP research can be divided based on the data utilization: works with large amounts of data and those with smaller, carefully processed datasets. The latter has been particularly useful for experimentally assessing various model components and developing novel architectures. However, with the introduction of deep neural networks that can achieve high performance on large datasets, the interest in studying small datasets has waned. These networks typically employ numerous parameters relative to the data points, leading to issues like data contamination and overfitting. We believe NLP researchers should explore developing novel regularization techniques suitable for training with public Gigabyte-scale datasets, thereby bridging the gap between works with moderate datasets and those with significantly larger corpora.

on a quantum computer, we modify the quantum imaginary time evolution (QITE) to utilize the model space. This model-space QITE method iteratively expands the model space while maintaining orthogonality and maintaining the energy above the model space. We show that this modified approach converges to a set of target states that can be verified to meet the requirements of the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) for exact targets. We find a specific scaling of Bose-Einstein condensation fractions in ground states that can be used to analyze quasi-condensation in weakly coupled quantum double dark-soliton states. We first demonstrate the precise time-dependent density profile of a quantum double dark-soliton state via the Bethe ansatz method. Next, we derive an effective macroscopic wave function for these states by calculating the amplitude and phase of field operator matrix elements. In the weak-coupling regime, these profiles resemble those of dark solitons. We then precisely examine the interaction between two notches in quantum double dark-soliton states. Observations suggest that quasi-condensation may play a significant role in quantum double dark-soliton dynamics. We also find that the notional energy of states precisely predicts the phase evolution of states, providing strong evidence that phase dynamics are driven by quasi-condensation in the quantum double dark-soliton system.

single-phase Darcy flow within a fractured porous media, incorporating two types of fractures. These fractures can be oriented in any configuration and may intersect, but fluid cannot flow across their interfaces. The proposed method uses two different polynomial spaces for pressure and velocity across the fractures and eliminates the need to match normal velocities and pressures across the interfaces, greatly simplifying implementation. Mass conservation across the interfaces is maintained by adjusting the fractures' velocities and pressures based on the pressure drop. A key feature of this approach, with minimal cross-talk between elements, allows for an easy-to-implement multigrid solver that works effectively for large problems. Mathematical analysis proves a second-order convergence rate for solutions as the mesh becomes finer, and multiple examples illustrate its efficiency and ease of use. This method also outperforms existing mass-conservative approaches in terms of computational efficiency.

It can be expressed through rule learning, which is characterized by the discovery of concise "if-then" statements that represent generalizable connections between antecedents and hypotheses. Traditional supervised learning approaches train classifiers using a labeled dataset to confirm the validity of pre-formulated hypotheses. In contrast, this study introduces a novel method for deriving if-then rules from training data that test given hypotheses, drawing inspiration from existing rule learning techniques. The proposed approach, defined as hypothesis testing, is an under-researched area that requires further exploration. Given the shared underlying mathematics of rule learning and hypothesis testing methods, we designed a flexible framework for hypothesis testing, which we applied to develop a high-performing rule learning algorithm. Notably, this method is capable of testing complex continuous hypotheses and demonstrates its effectiveness by outperforming existing state-of-the-art models in terms of accuracy and rule conciseness.

To improve the effectiveness of sentence representations in classification tasks, research has been done on predicting these indicators between sentences. This work diverges from this approach by using a trained model to forecast suitable indicators between sentences that have an established semantic connection, based on an input sentence and its subsequent sentence. This task, known as discriminative sentence prediction (DSP), presents significant challenges due to the variety of possible indicators and the unequal frequency of their occurrence. These issues lead to a biased output distribution and make it difficult for existing sequences models to excel at this task. To address these difficulties, an alternative strategy is proposed that focuses on a selective subset of frequently occurring indicators, allowing the model to develop criteria for choosing between this reduced set. To incorporate external knowledge about the indicators, the concept of local sentence type is introduced, which describes the general relationship between sentences and can be directly inferred from the input indicator. This information is used to guide the output distribution and create a more balanced approach to the task. These strategies are effective, showing improvements over existing sequences models on a publicly available test set.

Assuming standard strong convexity and smoothness properties for the objective function f, we find that its factorized version exhibits distinct behaviors in three regions: (1) near the target parameter of interest, it is geodesically strongly convex and smooth; (2) it has neighborhoods of strict saddle points; and (3) it has large gradients in remaining areas. Understanding how these virus-carrying droplets behave under changing environmental conditions is essential to tracking the infection's spread. To investigate this, we examine the movement of droplets released into varying wind environments, analyzing how they break up and dispersing in still air, gentle breezes and stronger winds. Our analysis includes describing the change in ambient wind as it affects the air around the droplets and how this influences their movement. We derived a mathematical expression to model the gradient wind effect and observed that even minor breezes can cause significant rotation larger droplets as they break up. rotation undergoes significant changes, following distinct phases. Upon reaching the zero-age main sequence, its overall rotational velocity slows down, adhering to Skumanich's law and making gyrochronology possible. As they age, some solar-type stars may eventually transition out of this braking phase. Additionally, 3D simulations of these stars have identified various differential rotation patterns, characterized by the Rossby number. Specifically, anti-solar differential rotation, characterized by rapid polar rotation and slow equatorial rotation, can occur in high-Rossby-number, slowly rotating stars. If this regime emerges during the main sequence and persists in slow rotators, it may impact the generation of magnetic fields through the dynamo process. Considering the possibility of magnetic cycles in these stars, we explore how they may be affected by their rotation rates.

Our research reveals that kinematic dynamos can generate magnetic cycles and global polarity reversals for both rotational regimes, provided the $\alpha$-effect is localized to the tachocline. However, when the $\alpha$-effect is distributed across the convection zone, solar-type cases exhibit magnetic cycles, whereas anti-solar cases do not. Traditional Babcock-Leighton flux-transport dynamos are unable to sustain magnetic cycles in anti-solar cases due to flux accumulation. Nevertheless, we propose that a memory-less flux-transport dynamo with a flip condition could still generate magnetic cycles in such stars, albeit with limited polarity reversal.

's atmosphere, examining how its composition has been shaped by interior-exterior interactions over time. Despite significant ongoing research, key aspects of the atmosphere's formation and current state remain unclear and require interdisciplinary analysis. We examine various processes that have influenced the atmosphere's evolution, starting with volatile sources and examining interactions from the planet's core to its upper atmosphere, as well as atmospheric escape mechanisms. We also delve into the complex historical events that have contributed to the atmosphere's evolution, including the effects of impacts, magnetic field generation, and geochemical and geodynamic feedback cycles. We then outline plausible pathways for the planet's evolution, ranging from its accretion phase to its present state, using modeling and observations. These scenarios include atmospheric escape during the magma ocean phase, prolonged surface liquid water that eventually gave way to a runaway greenhouse phase, and water retained within the planet due to inefficient outgassing, leading to hydrogen entrapment in the core and mantle oxidation. We review the existing evidence and discuss the need for future research, as well as potential observations and missions required to better understand Venus's complex interior, surface, and atmospheric interactions and how they have influenced the planet's evolution and future.

and patient outcomes depends heavily on the collaborative efforts of multiple healthcare professionals who rely on rich information exchange. Although professional communication can significantly impact patient care and safety, there is little current research that examines the quality and content of communication within the healthcare profession among doctors, nurses, and other medical staff. As a result, the development of effective, efficient, and safe AI tools for clinical settings is impeded due to a lack of necessary information. To address this critical knowledge gap and pave the way for more targeted evaluations, interventions, and the creation of high-performing AI systems, this research systematically identifies, maps, and synthesizes existing literature on the characteristics of communication within the healthcare profession across various contexts and settings. Our comprehensive findings highlight significant variations in the features of communication across different contexts and settings that affect professional collaboration and the performance of collaborative systems. Notable patterns have also been consistently observed across a range of settings and are categorised into seven key dimensions: information technology usage, real-time interaction, language usage, non-verbal communication, feedback mechanisms, learning opportunities, and feedback mechanisms. Our work provides the most complete overview to date of the dimensions, features, and features of communication within the healthcare profession across various contexts and settings, including associated performance metrics for collaborative systems. Ultimately, our findings highlight the significant variations that exist in communication and emphasize the critical dimensions and dimensions that need to be considered in order to develop effective, efficient, and safe AI tools for clinical settings.

Combining these detections with electromagnetic radiation holds significant potential to improve our comprehension of neutron star events, particularly their dense matter state. However, electromagnetic analysis of gravitational waves necessitates the rapid identification of signals from gravitational waves in real-time. Traditional approaches struggle to achieve this at the rate expected for future detectors. We introduce novel results based on a deep learning approach, which employs a convolutional neural network to classify signals from real LIGO data involving neutron star and black hole mergers. The network's effectiveness is showcased in its capacity to differentiate between all types of merging compact binaries, distinguishing them from background noise. Pyroptosis is primarily initiated through the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation which can be triggered by SARS-CoV-2 infection. Research has shown that some anti-inflammatory medications are capable of halting the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation, thereby delaying pyroptosis cell death. Our study develops a single-cell mathematical model to analyze the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation, cell death due to pyroptosis, and how these processes can be affected by medication. Formulated in terms of ordinary differential equations, the model uses experimental data for parameter estimation and further assumes a linear relationship between NLRP3 inflammasome levels and pyroptotic cell death, as well as the efficacy of medication. Sensitivity analysis of the model reveals that cells are most sensitive to changes in pyroptotic death coefficients and least sensitive to medication efficacy changes. Model simulations indicate that medication can decrease pyroptotic cell death, supported by additional analysis including parameter perturbation, delay equations, and actual clinical data. Ultimately, our study suggests that targeting pyroptosis may be a viable approach for treating COVID-19, and that further implementation of our model is possible with the inclusion of additional biological and medical factors.

al Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align input data with predetermined features, providing a cohesive framework that includes the analysis of non-linear elements like ReLU and max-pooling. A thorough exploration of feature extraction in deep GCNN architectures is then presented, followed by an examination of how they contribute to effective data classification, ultimately proving that certain components of complex GCNN systems can be represented as filter banks and utilized for classification purposes on their own.

Furthermore, our research provides a logical extension of this reasoning to account for the influence of other common components in modern deep GCNN systems, specifically volume reduction and attention mechanisms. We examine how max pooling and 1x1 convolutions contribute to feature selection and weighting within these systems. Our analysis is supported by supporting equations and illustrative examples designed to clarify often misinterpreted aspects of 1x1 convolutions and attention components.

a particular n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ within the range [0,1] is classified as 'cyclic' when there exist unique, independent random variables $(U_1, \ldots, U_n)$ where the likelihood of $U_{i+1}$ being greater than $U_i$ is $x_i$ for $i$ ranging from 1 to n-1, and the likelihood of $U_1$ being greater than $U_n$ is $x_n$. If this condition, combined with the additional stipulation that all individual elements $x_i$ be greater than 0.5, is satisfied, the n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ is classified as 'nontransitive'. 

We represent the likelihood of selecting a random n-tuple that meets these 'cyclic' criteria as $p_n$ and its 'nontransitive' counterpart as $p_n^*$. In our analysis, we find the actual values of $p_4$, $p_5$, and $p_n^*$ for $n$ equaling 4, 5, and any n greater than 3, respectively. Notably, the value of $p_n^*$ illuminates a previously unexplored facet of the famous Condorcet's voting paradox.

A key method in this area, the unsupervised cycleGAN approach, has demonstrated great promise in upgrading the quality of low-dose images without needing matched high-dose images as reference data. However, the use of two neural network generators in the training process is a significant limitation, primarily because the extra generator adds complexity and memory demands. In response to these issues, we have introduced a new cycleGAN framework based on a single, adaptive switchable generator. By incorporating adaptive instance normalization (AdaIN) layers, the baseline generator can efficiently transform a low-dose CT image into a routine-dose CT image and then easily switch to generating high-dose images from low-dose images simply by modifying the AdaIN codes. The proposed architecture achieves these conversions while minimizing the memory requirement and weight increase associated with additional generators, and can therefore be trained with more stability using limited training data. Our results demonstrate that the new method not only rivals but outperforms previous cycleGAN methods while needing only roughly half as many parameters.

This study proposes a new method for computing scattering cross-sections in lepton collisions, called final-state luminosity function formulation (FLFF). FLFF is a theoretical framework that extends the traditional parton model, which is based on the concept of hadron constituents in protons to include the lepton's photon fluctuations at high-energy. This framework allows the traditional parton-model-based computation methods, such as the Neumann method for handling higher-order corrections, to be applied to lepton collisions. The paper presents several examples of cross-section calculations in the FLFF context, including the probability of a photon reaching a certain energy fraction of the total lepton energy and how this is affected by the order of perturbation theory used. The implications of using the FLFF for computing cross-sections in high-energy lepton collisions are also poked at.

To overcome this limitation, researchers have explored the potential of multi-hop directional transmission techniques to extend communication range, albeit these schemes can result in prolonged beam training time using conventional methods such as exhaustive search or hierarchical approaches. To tackle this problem, a novel hierarchical beam training technique is proposed in this paper that dynamically optimizes training levels across individual single-hop links, maximizing overall spectral efficiency. To tackle this optimization problem in the presence of channel state uncertainty and noise, a reinforcement learning solution inspired by the multi-armed bandit problem is proposed. Simulations show the new technique converges quickly in dynamic channel conditions and offers up to 75% better performance than conventional methods in terms of spectral efficiency.

Consequently, there's growing interest in learning how these worlds receive radiation and radiation-induced chemical transformations within their atmospheres, which may eventually affect the signals detected by space telescopes. This study focuses on modeling the atmospheric chemistry of super-Earths orbiting low-luminosity stars, specifically K5V stars, and how dimmer light sources affect it. Using the KOPKOP transit radiation model and the REM model, we examined the chemical composition of the atmospheres of two planets, orbiting the K5V star, at 10 times their equilibrium temperature. Our analysis of possible biosignatures like $H_2O$, $O_2$, $O_3$, $CH_4$, $CH_3OH$, $N_2O$, and $NO_2$ showed that key molecules such as $O_2$, $O_3$, $CH_4$, and $NO_2$ are largely undetectable. Notably, the reduction in stellar luminosity causes $NO_2$ to become less accessible at lower temperatures, whereas the detectability of $CH_4$ becomes dependent on the star's luminosity. This research has significant implications for understanding the atmospheres of planets orbiting dimmer stars and could influence future spectroscopic studies.

Researchers have proposed GCNs in non-Euclidean geometry, specifically in hyperbolic space, and have achieved notable performance improvements. However, existing hyperbolic graph operations fail to accurately follow the principles of hyperbolic geometry, potentially hindering the efficacy of these networks. This paper presents a novel hyperbolic GCN called Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) that ensures learned node features adhere to hyperbolic geometry. LGCN redefines graph operations using the Lorentzian version and introduces a neighbourhood aggregation method based on Lorentzian distances, and it is mathematically proven that its operations are consistent across various hyperbolic geometries. Experimental evaluations on six datasets demonstrate LGCN's superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, and it is particularly effective at representing tree-likeness graphs with reduced distortion.

In chosndrites, the hydrogen isotope values in pyroxene minerals from different formations vary but water content values are consistent. In shergottites, hydrogen isotope values in pyroxene minerals from different formations are similar, but the water content values vary significantly. The hydrogen found in the pyroxene minerals of martian origin likely came from sources similar to those in chondrites, including volatiles present during the solar nebula, the martian atmosphere, and possibly water found within the martian crust. The water found in the pyroxene minerals of shergottites may have resulted from the original water present in the martian nebula, the martian atmosphere, and possibly water found within the martian crust. As a result, the water content found in the pyroxene minerals of shergottites may indicate the presence of up to several hundred parts per million of water found within the martian crust.

By contrast, single-system approaches reduce errors but are complicated to deploy due to limited data availability. We delve into zero-shot translation, which allows for language pairs that weren't encountered during training, thereby circumventing the need for speech-to-text data. While this method has been explored before for speech-to-text translation, it's typically limited to pairs from the same language family. Our research takes it a step further by conducting zero-shot translation across unrelated languages. We employed fMLP and Cross-lingual Speech Recognition (CSR) frameworks for this purpose and found that our zero-shot translation achieved comparable performance to Cross-lingual Speech-to-Text (CSST) in contact language pairs. In non-contact language pairs, the results demonstrated the feasibility of achieving meaningful results, although further research is needed. Our experiments also revealed that the choice of speech recognition model significantly impacts performance. Overall, our study showcases successful translation of spoken language across diverse language barriers.

By integrating the minimal dark sector into the simplest "missing partner" type-I seesaw framework, we establish a comprehensive understanding of neutrino oscillation lengths and dark matter abundance through their interactions with the new scalar field responsible for the seesaw mechanism. Our analysis, constrained by the dark matter relic density, direct detection limits, the cosmic microwave background, and neutrino masses obtained from the seesaw Lagrangian parameters at the electroweak scale, reveals that the new particle's mass must lie within a specific range of 4.6 TeV to 100 TeV to also satisfy the neutrino particle length requirements. This analysis is underpinned by an evaluation of the variable mass neutrino decay rates using the measured neutrino mass squared differences and masses, providing predictions for the possible detection of coherent neutrino scattering from ultra-high energy neutrinos with possible future experiments like IceCube-Gen2, CNAO, DUNE, and Hyper-Kamiokande.

By directly comparing with $t_{2g}$ only or $e_g$ only models based on electron filling, we investigate the magnetic properties of all possible $d$-shell configurations, incorporating calculations of the total magnetic moment, orbital occupation, and effective spin-orbit coupling. In this research, a concept for GAN-based medical imaging enhancement is demonstrated. Though GAN-based techniques excel at natural image creation and manipulation, their potential in medicine remains largely unexplored. Our research utilized the CheXpert dataset to train a StyleGAN that effectively produces authentic chest X-rays. By incorporating an encoder from the Cyclic Reverse Generator framework, we successfully developed an inverse mapping system to recreate synthetic X-rays accurately and reconstruct organs on real X-rays. By fine-tuning latent codes, we successfully transplanted a cardiac enlargement condition onto normal chest X-rays. Our research was showcased at the Medical Imaging meets NeurIPS Workshop 2020, a satellite event of the 34th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems held in Vancouver, Canada.

For domains with irregular boundaries, using a grid without a set pattern to represent the potential function brings significant computational and storage benefits. However, computing these potentials for distant points from the domain requires addressing challenges related to stable algorithms. We've developed such an algorithm in a previous study, but it relied on the potential at the origin as a starting point, which isn't always optimal, especially when the origin is close to or within the domain. Our new algorithm extends this previous work by finding the best point to begin calculations from, thus making it more suitable for solving integral equations. This involves determining the point that maximizes the distance from the domain, which leads to more accurate and stable computations.
